articleTitle: Hybrid excitation of AC and DC machines
publicationTitle: 1989 Fourth International Conference on Electrical Machines and Drives Conf. Publ. No. ??)
abstract: The authors demonstrate that the straightforward combination of surface-mounted magnets and a conventional field coil is unlikely to bring any benefit in most small machines where airgaps are dictated by mechanical clearance requirements. In larger machines where armature-reaction demands a larger gap, hybrid excitation can be worthwhile and it is shown that economical use of the expensive magnet material can be achieved with a layer covering only part of the pole surface. In machines of the transverse-flux or homopolar type, a very large improvement in utilisation of material is found when a hybrid excitation arrangement is used, even with cheap ferrite magnets.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Comparison of design and performance parameters in switched reluctance and induction motors
publicationTitle: 1989 Fourth International Conference on Electrical Machines and Drives Conf. Publ. No. ??)
abstract: The switched reluctance motor is now widely recognised as an important class of machine, offering the potential for variable speed drive systems that are competitive with those based on the induction motor and other classical machine types. Here, the authors present a comparison of the design and performance of these two machines, which shows clearly the switched reluctance motor has much to offer in terms of performance advantage. It slightly exceeds the efficiency of the high-efficiency induction motor, and at the same time greatly excels it on all measures relating to specific output. However, it is significantly inferior to the standard-efficiency induction motor on torque per unit stator core volume, temperature rise and noise.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: A diagnostic system for three-phase asynchronous machines
publicationTitle: 1989 Fourth International Conference on Electrical Machines and Drives Conf. Publ. No. ??)
abstract: The authors present a brand-new diagnostic system for three-phase induction machines as well cage and slipring motors which allows one to protect the machine against all faults of practical importance within the active parts. The faults include all kinds of winding damage, rotor eccentricity, and rotor unsymmetry in the case of cage motors (e.g. broken bars or end rings). The system also distinguishes and monitors the different faults by using one measuring element only.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: The vibrational behaviour of laminated components in electrical machines
publicationTitle: 1989 Fourth International Conference on Electrical Machines and Drives Conf. Publ. No. ??)
abstract: The author illustrates that laminated components are very significantly more flexible than their solid counterparts in some respects and that this fact has a strong bearing on the levels of vibration which occur in an electrical machine. The author presents some data which will provide estimates for the various moduli which determine the stiffness of a laminated structure. A method for experimentally determining flexibilities so that manufacturers have a straightforward technique for determining what values of the moduli ought be applied to their machines is formalised.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Fault detection in induction motors as a result of transient analysis
publicationTitle: 1989 Fourth International Conference on Electrical Machines and Drives Conf. Publ. No. ??)
abstract: A technique is being developed which will allow the detection and identification of specific faults within 3-phase induction motors during the starting transient. At present a very detailed and complex analysis is used to detect faults requiring the use of a mainframe computer. It is anticipated that once sufficient test data has been obtained this analysis will be dramatically reduced, allowing a stand alone instrument to be designed.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Analysis of torque ripple in electronically commutated permanent magnet machines and minimization methods
publicationTitle: 1989 Fourth International Conference on Electrical Machines and Drives Conf. Publ. No. ??)
abstract: The authors deal with permanent magnet machines with rectangular induction and current waveforms. In order to minimize the machine torque ripple, the evolution of the torque curves of the different windings supplied with constant current in function of the position of the rotor, must have a trapezoidal shape comprising a plateau with the correct width. They must be correctly juxtaposed by an adequate choice of the supply sequences. Moreover, in order to get the most out of the torque, an optimal use of the air-gap must be made by making the largest number of conductors work simultaneously. The influence of different parameters on the constant current torque curve shape are examined. The different ways of combining these torque curves are analysed so as to come to the best use of the air-gap and minimize the resulting torque ripple at the same time.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Transient electrical and mechanical behaviour of large induction generator installations
publicationTitle: 1989 Fourth International Conference on Electrical Machines and Drives Conf. Publ. No. ??)
abstract: Induction generators in energy recovery schemes are an excellent economic choice, giving operationally simple and low maintenance service. Self excited units can offer low inrush synchronizing performance, well suited to soft supply systems. The use of permanently connected capacitors is found to be advantageous, despite potential harmonic current and transient effects. The process of self-excitation has operationally been found to be reliable, the use of effective start sequencing being important in this respect. Despite serious supply disturbance, an induction generator has been shown to be safe in operation when suitable protection measures have been taken.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Condition monitoring-the way ahead for large electrical machines
publicationTitle: 1989 Fourth International Conference on Electrical Machines and Drives Conf. Publ. No. ??)
abstract: The author describes the way ahead for the application of condition monitoring to large electrical machines for both installation on new machines, to assist in providing a long life, and retrofit installation on existing machines, to prolong their life in service as part of a refurbishment programme.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: An improved engine-testing dynamometer
publicationTitle: 1989 Fourth International Conference on Electrical Machines and Drives Conf. Publ. No. ??)
abstract: The authors show that the naturally commutated, converter-fed synchronous machine has features which make it particularly suited to being an engine testing dynamometer. The major part of the operating time of an engine testing dynamometer is likely to be in the absorbing mode, which in this case is a generating mode and one in which the system operates with a relatively high efficiency, a high degree of controllability and great reliability. A method is described whereby the potentially damaging effects of interruption of the mains, whilst in this mode, could be avoided.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: A frequency controller for induction generators in stand-by minihydro power plants
publicationTitle: 1989 Fourth International Conference on Electrical Machines and Drives Conf. Publ. No. ??)
abstract: Induction generators working in minihydro power plants separated from the main network have to maintain constant frequency for every load condition. The equilibrium between the torque generated by the turbine and the load torque has to be reached for the speed corresponding to the requested frequency. In the small power range plants (up to 500 kW), the solution with turbines without regulation can be economically attractive. However, an additional variable dissipative system in parallel to the main loads supplied by the induction generator has to be provided. A variable dissipative system controlled with continuity and not step by step can be realized utilizing a thyristor converter with resistive load. The thyristor firing signals have to be generated by a PID frequency controller. In order to avoid the problems of unbalanced voltage due to single phase loads or unsymmetrical three phases loads, a new digital controller for the variable dissipative load is proposed. The authors deal with the design of the overall system for a practical application.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Effects of end-shields and rotor on natural frequencies and modes of stator of small electrical machines
publicationTitle: 1989 Fourth International Conference on Electrical Machines and Drives Conf. Publ. No. ??)
abstract: The effects of allowing for the end-shields, the rotor and the running condition on the natural frequencies and modes of the stator of a small electrical machine have been investigated by the modern experimental modal analysis technique. It was been shown that: because of the restricting effects, the end-shields significantly increase the values of the natural frequencies of the stator; by comparison the effect of the rotor is much smaller, however the rotor does cause important new natural frequencies to be introduced, in particular the first-order mode; and the modifying effects under a no-load condition are negligible, as is also likely to be the case up to rated load. The study has provided data which should assist further investigations, particularly in regard to the effects of the mounting feet on the natural frequencies and modes of stators, in developing vibrational models based on finite elements, as well as acoustic models.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: MMF and permeance harmonic torques and losses in cage induction motors-the effects of skew, bar-to-bar impedance and saturation
publicationTitle: 1989 Fourth International Conference on Electrical Machines and Drives Conf. Publ. No. ??)
abstract: The overall machine analysis technique described has been based on an equivalent circuit representation of the induction motor. Methods of determining each additional component of loss have been outlined and the most useful approach has been found to be that based upon the solution of a series of harmonic equivalent circuits. In some cases simplified finite-element models have been found to be particularly useful in the determination of equivalent circuit parameters. The major sources of additional loss in inverter-fed machines have been identified as: additional stator winding loss arising from skin and proximity effects at high frequency; additional rotor winding loss arising from deep bar effects at high frequency; additional core loss due to the existence of harmonic fluxes; and additional stray loss.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Torque pulsations on inverter fed induction motors
publicationTitle: 1989 Fourth International Conference on Electrical Machines and Drives Conf. Publ. No. ??)
abstract: Following a review of large induction motor variable speed drive systems, the authors discuss air-gap torque pulsation characteristics. Measured noninteger current harmonics are shown, and the need to include them in total drive system design is identified. Some useful analytical methods are also presented.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Dynamic modelling and performance prediction of brushless permanent magnet drive systems
publicationTitle: 1989 Fourth International Conference on Electrical Machines and Drives Conf. Publ. No. ??)
abstract: Three-phase, trapezoidal-EMF, permanent magnet motors have been developed for many applications. However the design of a drive system often necessitates analysis of its dynamic behaviour, to establish that its performance, in terms of its torque-speed characteristic, torque and speed ripple, current spikes etc. will be acceptable. The simulation model described has the flexibility for modelling quite diverse supply conditions, including PWM or current mode, and back-EMF waveforms, as well as alternative control strategies. When coupled with the finite-element analysis of a motor therefore, from which parameters such as the EMF constant and waveform, winding inductances and a cogging torque function can be generated, the model allows the precise steady-state and transient performance to be predicted.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Transient unbalanced magnetic pull in change-pole induction motors
publicationTitle: 1989 Fourth International Conference on Electrical Machines and Drives Conf. Publ. No. ??)
abstract: In an ideal three-phase cage motor, which is both electrically and magnetically symmetrical, the radial forces acting on the rotor are in equilibrium, so that their resultant is zero. An out-of-balance radial force, usually referred to as an unbalance magnetic pull (UMP) arises when either or both forms of symmetry are disturbed. It is well-known that a transient UMP may be produced during pole switching in a machine which is fitted with either a pole-change winding or with two separate windings of different pole number. The force developed may be large enough to produce a pull over; that is the rotor and stator can come into physical contact. The authors explain and examine this phenomenon.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Use of flux screens in switched reluctance motors
publicationTitle: 1989 Fourth International Conference on Electrical Machines and Drives Conf. Publ. No. ??)
abstract: The authors explore the use of conducting screens to achieve a dynamic reduction in the effective minimum inductance of a switched reluctance (SR) motor by means of reactance-limited eddy currents. Several configurations of screen are examined, on both the rotor and the stator. Results calculated by finite-element analysis and dynamic simulation are compared with measurements made on a small SR motor.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: A canned solid rotor permanent magnet machine with skewed-radial neodymium-iron-boron magnets
publicationTitle: 1989 Fourth International Conference on Electrical Machines and Drives Conf. Publ. No. ??)
abstract: A permanent magnet machine has been constructed which consists of a solid steel rotor with six magnets which are mounted radially but skewed. The rotor magnets are skewed with respect to the stator slots. In addition, the rotor is surrounded by a nonmagnetic conducting can made of inconel. This strengthens the rotor which otherwise has significant speed limitations due to centrifugal force. The effect of skewing the rotor magnets is ro reduce torque harmonics and noise-producing flux components. The effect of the rotor can is beneficial, in addition to increasing the operating speed of the machine. The solid canned rotor is very stable and easy to manufacture.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: A new approach for measurement of the torque-speed characteristics of induction motors
publicationTitle: 1989 Fourth International Conference on Electrical Machines and Drives Conf. Publ. No. ??)
abstract: The authors present a new measurement technique for the determination of the torque-speed characteristics of induction motors. This technique is in compliance with the IEEE standard test procedure for polyphase induction motors and generators. The basic principle of this new approach consists of three main steps. The first is dynamic measurement of the speed as a function of time. The second is digital filtering of the raw speed data. Finally, the speed signal is numerically differentiated to obtain the acceleration from which the torque of the machine can be found. Experimental tests using two 20 HP induction motors confirmed that this approach is more advantageous than other methods. Also, the method produces accurate results over the full speed range of the machine in contrast to some other methods.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Benefits of Nd-Fe-B magnet in brushless DC motor design for aircraft applications
publicationTitle: 1989 Fourth International Conference on Electrical Machines and Drives Conf. Publ. No. ??)
abstract: Aircraft and defence applications require extremely compact designs which have the benefits of saving weight and space. These aspects demand motors of very high output power to weight ratio and reasonable high efficiency. There has seen a significant number of brushless DC motors being developed for the above applications. The author looks at the use of neodymium-iron-boron magnet in the design of brushless DC motors. The effect of high energy product of NdFeB is examined in relation to performance and frame size. Performance results of the motor with NdFeB for a typical practical application are presented. Design ideas relating to rotor geometries for a wide range of fan applications are described and shown to have significant improvement in both power to weight ratio and efficiency. Examples of practical drives are also presented.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Practical implementation and test facility for field orientated induction motor drives
publicationTitle: 1989 Fourth International Conference on Electrical Machines and Drives Conf. Publ. No. ??)
abstract: There has been much academic interest in field-orientated induction motor drives. The major aim of the research described is to apply the rapidly evolving techniques of modern control theory, particularly parameter identification, to such drives. Another aim is to advance the practical application of such schemes as have been developed, both here and elsewhere. To this practical end a comprehensive 32 bit microprocessor based data acquisition, computation and control system is being developed. This unit, with floating point coprocessor and hard disk, is based on a VMEbus rack system and has ample space for expansion to implement any likely future identification, measurement or control scheme. Machine drive is via a PWM inverter. The features of this novel system and test bed are described.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Development of a digital excitation control system
publicationTitle: 1989 Fourth International Conference on Electrical Machines and Drives Conf. Publ. No. ??)
abstract: Since 1985, NEI Parsons have been supplying digital governor control systems for the safe and reliable operation of new and refurbished turbogenerator plant. The techniques evolved for the digital governor, and subsequently proven in service, have been further developed into a unified range of microprocessor based control systems for flexible high-integrity control. The turbine is controlled by the electro-hydraulic governor, the generator is controlled by the automatic voltage regulator and both benefit by a sequence and monitoring system which provides automatic run-up and loading, on-load valve testing and thermal stress monitoring. The authors describe the important features of the digital automatic voltage regulator (AVR) control system. Triplex modular redundant (TMR) architecture is used in conjunction with majority voting of the outputs of three control channels to provide a high level of redundancy. Computer aided software engineering (CASE) tools were used with in-house software quality assurance procedures to develop the software.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Capacitor compensated variable speed induction motor drives
publicationTitle: 1989 Fourth International Conference on Electrical Machines and Drives Conf. Publ. No. ??)
abstract: Capacitor compensated variable speed induction drives (CCVSIDs) from 500 kW to 5 MW output capacity have been manufactured in substantial numbers during the past decade and have given reliable performance in a wide variety of commercial installations. They have been installed in chemical plant, oil exploration rigs, oil production platforms, oil refineries, paper mills, power stations, ships and in steel mills. Other applications to open up new business opportunities in traditional industries, are being developed. The authors outline briefly the principles underlying CCVSIDs and describes the approaches that are adopted to ensure that speed control of induction motors can be achieved with high reliability and integrity.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Calculation of the performances of a synchronous machine with salient solid poles using the boundary integral method
publicationTitle: 1989 Fourth International Conference on Electrical Machines and Drives Conf. Publ. No. ??)
abstract: The boundary integral method is very attractive by its simplicity of use, mainly when we are only interested to the solution on the domain boundary. The authors apply this method to a bipolar reluctance machine which has solid rotor poles, whose synchronous behaviour has been studied for a long time in their laboratory. The asynchronous starting is computed by the boundary integral method and compared with an experimental study.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Synchronous motors with Nd-Fe-B magnets and solid-steel rotor
publicationTitle: 1989 Fourth International Conference on Electrical Machines and Drives Conf. Publ. No. ??)
abstract: The authors present a study of an alternative form of rotor construction which uses a solid-steel body and blocks of magnet material located beneath steel pole caps. This enables rectangular pieces of magnet to be used and only the pole caps need be skewed to avoid cogging torques. Asynchronous starting torque is contributed by eddy currents induced in the solid-steel rotor, primarily in the pole caps.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Brushless NdFeB permanent magnet DC linear motors
publicationTitle: 1989 Fourth International Conference on Electrical Machines and Drives Conf. Publ. No. ??)
abstract: The authors describe several DC linear motors which are microprocessor controlled and as the field source, use NdFeB magnets, the newly developed high energy, rare earth permanent magnets. A ferrite-field DC linear motor is also described and its parameters are compared with those of the NdFeB-field motors.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Computational methods for the steady-state performance prediction of cage induction machines fed from nonsinusoidal supplies
publicationTitle: 1989 Fourth International Conference on Electrical Machines and Drives Conf. Publ. No. ??)
abstract: Cage induction motors can be supplied from various types of solid-state adjustable frequency controllers with a wide range of operating characteristics. However, the inverter/machine combination results in the necessity to derate the motor due to harmonic effects arising from the nonsinusoidal nature of the applied voltage. The overall magnitude and distribution of the additional loss and consequent reduction in motor rating depends on the harmonic content of the applied waveform, and on certain aspects of the machine design. Calculation of this additional loss requires a detailed knowledge of the current and flux redistributions which occur at high frequencies. A comprehensive study of the performance and design of inverter-fed machines is being undertaken at ERA as part of a major collaborative research programme. The authors summarise the general approach adopted in the study and outline suitable techniques for evaluating the major sources of additional loss.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Computation of torque pulsations of switched reluctance drive
publicationTitle: 1989 Fourth International Conference on Electrical Machines and Drives Conf. Publ. No. ??)
abstract: The switched reluctance (SR) drive exhibits torque pulsations (ripple) due to: (i) the constructional features of the machine-salient poles on both stator and rotor; and (ii) a switched form of supply. The form and level of torque pulsations are therefore dependent on variables related to the geometrical form of the magnetic circuit and on those related to the phase current waveform. The influence of these variables on torque pulsations can be estimated by sophisticated mathematical models. The authors describe a procedure for computing the instantaneous values of electromagnetic torque exhibiting pulsations. It is assumed that magnetic parameter data (inductances or flux-linkage against position and current) are known, i.e. the data are obtained by measurements in stall conditions or computed by numerical field analysis.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: The application of heat pipes to cooling rotating electrical machines
publicationTitle: 1989 Fourth International Conference on Electrical Machines and Drives Conf. Publ. No. ??)
abstract: A heat pipe is a closed system (normally tubular) containing: a material which is able to undergo a phase change, thus absorbing heat at one point within the system and redepositing it at any other point within the system which is at a lower temperature; and some means of returning the working material to the starting point so that a continuous cycle can be maintained. The author examines the possible application of heat pipes to electrical machines. The author discusses heat pipe operation including choice of working fluid and thermal resistance. The thermal characterisation of heat pipes is also discussed.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Two-dimensional leakage flux estimation in switched reluctance motors
publicationTitle: 1989 Fourth International Conference on Electrical Machines and Drives Conf. Publ. No. ??)
abstract: Components of flux inside a switched reluctance motor (SRM) which do not cross the airgap between the stator and rotor teeth (henceforth called leakage fluxes) can have a major effect on the performance of SRMs. In this paper, the flux pattern within three SRMs in the important unaligned position, is used to obtain analytical formulae for leakage flux estimation, both from the excited pole to the stator back of the core and to the adjacent stator pole. The results are then compared with those obtained by finite element analysis. The formulae obtained for leakage permeances relate these components of the permeance to the dimensions of the motors.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Development of novel instrumentation and expert system concepts in turbine generator condition monitoring
publicationTitle: 1989 Fourth International Conference on Electrical Machines and Drives Conf. Publ. No. ??)
abstract: Efforts to develop new diagnostic techniques to improve condition monitoring of turbine generators are described. Work is concentrated on those areas where deficiencies in existing instrumentation were identified. Improvements in assessment capability are also being sought through reduction in the false alarm rate of existing techniques and by better use of conventional sensor data by means of expert systems concepts.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Design analysis by finite-element time-stepping techniques
publicationTitle: 1989 Fourth International Conference on Electrical Machines and Drives Conf. Publ. No. ??)
abstract: It has become necessary to develop analysis techniques to predict losses, torque variation and the interaction between motors and inverters. The authors describe the development of a nonlinear finite-element time-stepping method which allows for the distribution of stator currents in slots, external circuits and rotor movement. To check the accuracy of the method, comparisons between test and calculations are made for an Exe induction motor at standstill and a synchronous motor operating from a current-fed inverter.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Some aspects of the electromagnetic design of a convertor-fed high speed synchronous motor
publicationTitle: 1989 Fourth International Conference on Electrical Machines and Drives Conf. Publ. No. ??)
abstract: The authors describe the principal design features of a typical high speed motor based on the 9 MW, 2-pole, 5600 r.p.m., 93.3 Hz motors supplied for the boiler-feed pumps of the Majuba Power Station in South Africa. The emphasis is on the electromagnetic design. Finite element field distribution methods are used to investigate various electromagnetic aspects of its design, and two cases of the application of these advanced methods are presented. The first example deals with the calculation of losses in the rotor due to the harmonic currents in the convertor supply. The second example illustrates the scheme of determination of reactances and time constants based on the finite element simulation of the standstill frequency injection tests, and compares the calculated results against those obtained from tests.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: A self-commutating PM machine with implicit rotor position sensing using search coils
publicationTitle: 1989 Fourth International Conference on Electrical Machines and Drives Conf. Publ. No. ??)
abstract: The detection of rotor position required for a self-commutating machine can be performed using search coils embedded in the stator, and without reference to any external encoder. The closed-loop speed control system is able to drive the motor accurately and at maximum efficiency for a wide range of speeds and loads, using the same search coil sensor technique for speed control as for the inverter switching. A complete self-contained drive system can therefore be built using this technique.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Design factors involved in mechanically coupling electrical machines to driving or driven equipment
publicationTitle: 1989 Fourth International Conference on Electrical Machines and Drives Conf. Publ. No. ??)
abstract: The loads to which electrical machines and coupled equipment can be subjected have been described. Appreciation of these loads and an understanding of the torsional characteristics of the coupled system as a whole is essential to the satisfactory performance of the equipment. Modern design aids can assist in identification of possible problem areas in system behaviour and the effects of proposed solutions can be assessed rapidly and effectively.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Instantaneous torque control brushless DC drives
publicationTitle: 1989 Fourth International Conference on Electrical Machines and Drives Conf. Publ. No. ??)
abstract: Permanent-magnet brushless DC drives can have excellent performance in direct-drive servo applications provided suitable control techniques are implemented. This calls for a cascade control strategy in which the controller is divided into two control loops: an outer loop which generates the instantaneous torque reference signal required to track acceleration, velocity or position; and an inner loop which forces the developed instantaneous torque to follow the torque command. In most conventional control algorithms, the inner loop is designed to produce sinusoidal stator currents, thus giving rise to significant torque ripples if the motor has a back EMF waveform which differs appreciably from the ideal sinusoid. A digital torque control scheme is proposed which uses the variable structure approach to generate the on-off switching patterns (vectors) directly with a microprocessor. At every switching instant, the optimum vector is selected to force the developed torque to follow the torque reference while keeping the direct axis current as close to zero as possible for the highest efficiency. The instantaneous torque feedback signal can be estimated from the terminal quantities of the motor. Simulation results are presented.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Turbogenerator electromagnetic design-the design of eddy current shields for screening of end-regions
publicationTitle: 1989 Fourth International Conference on Electrical Machines and Drives Conf. Publ. No. ??)
abstract: The author discusses the design of eddy current shields for turbogenerators. Using the finite element method the influence of shield thickness upon both the effectiveness of screening and the losses in the shield itself have been investigated. Results indicate that appreciable screening still takes place even when the shield is reduced to a thickness considerably less than one skin depth, but that such a thin shield will incur high eddy current losses. Work on wrap-around shields shows them to be effective in screening the inner radius of the stator core end plate. They also reduce stator core back axial flux, but this is accompanied by a modest increase in stator tooth axial fluxes. Losses in wrap-around shields are considerably greater than in their flat counterparts.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Vector control of AC permanent magnet machines
publicationTitle: 1989 Fourth International Conference on Electrical Machines and Drives Conf. Publ. No. ??)
abstract: The author discusses the techniques of implementing vector control on a sinusoidal as well as on a trapezoidal back EMF AC permanent magnet machine. The vector diagram is used to clarify the operation of the former while the appropriate timing of the motor current with respect to the trapezoidal back EMF is emphasized in the latter. Results are presented to show the performance of both types of vector controlled PM motors.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Generalised predictive control applied to a turbogenerator voltage regulator
publicationTitle: 1989 Fourth International Conference on Electrical Machines and Drives Conf. Publ. No. ??)
abstract: The automatic voltage regulator (AVR) is an integral part of the turbo-generator's excitation control system. It controls the generator terminal voltage whilst ensuring proper sharing of the reactive power amongst parallel connected generators. Consequently the AVR must be designed to operate under various load and fault conditions. These dynamic changes can degrade the performance of generator excitation systems when conventional fixed-gain linear voltage regulators are used. The use of a self-tuning strategy for voltage regulation is shown to handle this problem well. The development of such a controller using microprocessor hardware is described, using an algorithm based on the generalised predictive control (GPC) strategy. Using a comprehensive simulator, it is shown that the system performance under fault condition is satisfactory. Finally, the performance of the controller is evaluated by implementation on a laboratory model turbo-generator.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Comparative analysis and parameter sensitivity of field oriented speed controlled asynchronous motors
publicationTitle: 1989 Fourth International Conference on Electrical Machines and Drives Conf. Publ. No. ??)
abstract: The authors present an introduction to sensitivity analysis and to output stability of controlled asynchronous motors. It is shown that both calculus procedures represent an important preliminary analysis to be performed for all controlled electrical motors to define the suitable accuracy of the used control technique and to evaluate the proper accuracy required to control loop components in agreement with the accuracy of the technique. The authors deal with sensitivity analysis for vectorial algorithm controlled asynchronous motors and summarize with particular emphasis on the more useful results obtained for the well-known field oriented control technique. Formal expressions are given for electromagnetic torque variations, which follow the uncertainty in motor parameter identification and the deviation of the phase of the input motor current instantaneous symmetrical component.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Performance and design of generators for combined cycle power plants
publicationTitle: 1989 Fourth International Conference on Electrical Machines and Drives Conf. Publ. No. ??)
abstract: In various countries there is a trend away from nuclear power plants. This change if oriented to power plants where the size of the turbogenerator units is below 200 MW. These power stations combine the gas and steam turbine cycles and offer the highest efficiency and subsequently the best utilisation of fuel. All components, including the generators, that have a cycling duty with high number of working hours, are optimised to achieve longer service life and enhanced reliability for capital goods. Besides, for more economical operation of the plants, the electrical efficiency of these machines must be very high. The author describes the performance of these generators and makes a comparison between the air and hydrogen cooled-type.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Transient performance prediction of electrical drives including the mechanical transmission system
publicationTitle: 1989 Fourth International Conference on Electrical Machines and Drives Conf. Publ. No. ??)
abstract: The transient behaviour of drive systems is investigated by means of simulation models and experimental work. The simulation models are very versatile and cater for a large number of operating modes. Various effects, both linear and nonlinear, are considered during the development of the simulation models. Various measuring systems are developed to measure the mechanical system variables and the effectiveness of these systems is illustrated. As illustrated there is good correlation between simulation and experimental results, providing a useful tool in the design of drive systems operating under dynamic conditions. Further work is at present in progress, aimed mainly at the improvement of the measuring systems as well as the investigating of other transient regimes in drive systems.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: CAD representation of variable speed drives for downhole pump applications
publicationTitle: 1989 Fourth International Conference on Electrical Machines and Drives Conf. Publ. No. ??)
abstract: The authors illustrate the usefulness of a CAD package, Silvar Lisco, for the simulation of variable speed drives including the type used for downhole pump applications on oil production sites. This complete software package was conceived to aid in the design of VLSI circuits. However one of the subroutines ANDI has been found to be powerful in the simulation of power electronic circuits and in particular machine variable speed drives. This type of software is particularly useful because of its graphical input of electrical circuits and its graphical output of results.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Vibration behaviour of short laminated stators of electrical machines and validity of simplified frequency equation
publicationTitle: 1989 Fourth International Conference on Electrical Machines and Drives Conf. Publ. No. ??)
abstract: The general frequency equation is applied to different laminated short stator models without windings, with windings, and with windings and impregnation. Also, the validity of the simplified frequency equation compared with that of the general frequency equation is studied. The results given by these two frequency equations are compared with the measured values for several models.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Comparison of finite element methods for turbine generator negative sequence performance prediction
publicationTitle: 1989 Fourth International Conference on Electrical Machines and Drives Conf. Publ. No. ??)
abstract: Line-to-line short circuits impose a substantial thermal loading on a turbine generator rotor as a result of the eddy current heating arising from negative sequence and direct currents. The temperatures produced may be large enough to cause a reduction in the strength of the rotor wedges, and to induce high thermal stresses at the corners of inertia slits. The authors demonstrate that provided accurate equivalent circuit parameters are available, the full time-stepping transient finite-element method for calculating negative sequence heating effects shows no significant advantage over the simpler mixed finite-element/equivalent circuit pseudo-steady-state method.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Influence of saturation on the dynamic performance of vector-controlled salient-pole synchronous machines
publicationTitle: 1989 Fourth International Conference on Electrical Machines and Drives Conf. Publ. No. ??)
abstract: The influence of saturation on the dynamic performance of a vector-controlled salient-pole synchronous machine has been investigated. The design of the current controllers has been based on state-variable approach, but using a linear machine model. Results of computer simulations based on the linear model show that the implemented current control yields optimal control response both at standstill and during acceleration. However, these results are too optimistic since in reality saturation plays an important role as experimentally verified. The control system has been implemented on a 5 kW synchronous machine drive and experimental results have been obtained which show that the implemented control system gives optimal control response for a certain set of parameters at a certain level of saturation. However, it is shown that the control response is not optimal if the saturation level is changed without retuning the controllers. It follows that optimal current control requires the application of adaptive controllers.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Dynamical stability of synchronous generators under torsional interaction
publicationTitle: 1989 Fourth International Conference on Electrical Machines and Drives Conf. Publ. No. ??)
abstract: It is known that three completely different aspects, i.e., induction generator effect, torsional interaction and transient torque, are concerned in subsynchronous resonance of a power system. Both electrical and mechanical dynamic processes are involved in torsional interaction, and there exist both electrical and mechanical self excitation. Practically, it is very difficult to separate the induction generator effect from the torsional interaction. Generally, torsional interaction will play the main role when the frequency of the subsynchronous alternating torque approaches any one of the natural frequencies of torsional vibration. On basis of the time-domain technique of perturbation analysis, the torsional interaction has been studied. With the time domain method, the force-free or transient component caused by the system itself can be taken into account besides the forced component of the oscillation. As the product of the increments is not neglected in the perturbation analysis, the interactions between every component of oscillation are also considered.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: A frequency domain method for small signal turbogenerator and power system stabiliser studies
publicationTitle: 1989 Fourth International Conference on Electrical Machines and Drives Conf. Publ. No. ??)
abstract: This method directly uses generator frequency domain data and treats all the auxiliary systems in terms of frequency transfer functions. It has the advantage of being computationally efficient and accurate. It is also capable of modelling very complicated systems without needing extra computing power. This method can be applied to the following areas: investigation of the effect of power system stabilizer and AVR parameters on the system transient stability; study of system stability as affected by machine loading conditions; examination of transmission line effect on machine transient responses; and research into generator performance as affected by its physical design.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: An experimental study of the pressure drop in generator rotor cooling ducts
publicationTitle: 1989 Fourth International Conference on Electrical Machines and Drives Conf. Publ. No. ??)
abstract: The rotor windings of large generators are usually cooled by hydrogen flowing through ducts within the winding. To obtain fundamental information on the flow and heat transfer behaviour of such cooling ducts, a rig has been constructed at the Central Electricity Research Laboratories to study a heated duct rotating about a parallel axis. Results obtained so far suggest an increase in friction factor of about 10% for fully-developed flow in a heated duct, for conditions corresponding to those in large generators.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Efficient approach to dynamic modelling and transient analysis of SCR-controlled induction motors
publicationTitle: 1989 Fourth International Conference on Electrical Machines and Drives Conf. Publ. No. ??)
abstract: In this paper, a direct three-phase model is used in the transient performance analysis of a three-phase induction motor with SCR-controlled supply. The model elaborated enables the prediction of motor performance in both transient and steady-state operating conditions without the need to invert the machine inductance matrix during the calculations which avoids the only inconvenience of this method. Numerical and practical results are given.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Designs for the 1990s (electric machines)
publicationTitle: 1989 Fourth International Conference on Electrical Machines and Drives Conf. Publ. No. ??)
abstract: Customers are imposing increasingly arduous performance criteria on the electric machines which they order to meet all criteria simultaneously can often require highly optimised designs. In order to create these designs effectively, data from acceptance tests must be returned to the designers in a form which can be used to compare with the theoretical design. Furthermore, in order to carry out economic optimisation, manufacturing details must be made available to the designer.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Magnetic rotary position encoders with magneto-resistive sensors
publicationTitle: 1989 Fourth International Conference on Electrical Machines and Drives Conf. Publ. No. ??)
abstract: The performance of magnetic encoders is now comparable to optical types for many motion control applications. Magnetic recording techniques are used to establish high density tracks with uniform pole structures on isotropic permanent magnet media. The flux reversals are sensed using magneto-resistive elements, which allow quadrature incremental and index encoder channels to be derived from a single thick-film sensor.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Voltage surges in excitation circuits of contactless synchronous alternators-causes and prevention
publicationTitle: 1989 Fourth International Conference on Electrical Machines and Drives Conf. Publ. No. ??)
abstract: There are many potential causes of transient conditions leading to overvoltages in contactless synchronous alternators. One of them is faulty synchronizing. The authors investigate many cases where, due to such a cause, serious damage to the exciter armature winding took place after the breakdown of the diode. The analysis of conditions leading to the voltage surges during connection of the generator to the system is presented as well as suggestions of how to avoid them.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Application of dead time compensation to variable speed drives
publicationTitle: 1989 Fourth International Conference on Electrical Machines and Drives Conf. Publ. No. ??)
abstract: The performance of a variable speed drive system is analysed in terms of its output torque characteristics. As a consequence of introducing dead times, the output voltage applied to the motor load has a reduced fundamental voltage component and added unwanted low order voltage harmonics. The effect of reducing the fundamental voltage causes both a step change in torque over a gear change and a reduction of the steady state output torque. Compensating for dead time results in a negligible torque perturbation when gear changing and an increased steady state torque, although this torque is still less than the ideal at low frequency due to the effect of the motor's stator resistance.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: The modelling of synchronous machines
publicationTitle: 1989 Fourth International Conference on Electrical Machines and Drives Conf. Publ. No. ??)
abstract: Frequency response methods are becoming the standard means for the determination of the parameters of synchronous machines for transient stability studies. A new procedure for the determination of the time constants required to fit the frequency responses of the measured operational inductances of synchronous machines is described. The procedure does not require prior knowledge of the order of the model to be used, it is founded on well established principles of linear control theory and is found to work well for the equivalent circuits used for synchronous machines.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Representation of damper bars in computer models of synchronous motors supplied from variable frequency inverters
publicationTitle: 1989 Fourth International Conference on Electrical Machines and Drives Conf. Publ. No. ??)
abstract: The authors investigate the modelling of damper windings to predict damper currents in variable speed drives. In this type of drive two simple thyristor line-commutated bridges supply a synchronous machine. The machine is over-excited to produce a leading input power factor, and in this condition the terminal voltage of the machine is capable of providing natural commutation of the output thyristor bridge. The lack of forced commutation results in a relatively simple variable-speed drive using industrial grade thyristors. The action of the damper bars is critical to the performance of the drive and a computer programme is described which is capable of predicting the induced damper bar currents under saturated conditions.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Integrated technology of fractional horse power electrical machines
publicationTitle: 1989 Fourth International Conference on Electrical Machines and Drives Conf. Publ. No. ??)
abstract: An increase of electrical machines production requires seeking of new construction and technological solutions, particularly in the case of the fractional horse power machines. The integrated technology methods enable one to compact magnetic cores, manufacture of stator winding conductors and groove-teeth zones and to put conductors and groove insulators on by methods of layer deposition.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Application developments on unconventional AC drives
publicationTitle: 1989 Fourth International Conference on Electrical Machines and Drives Conf. Publ. No. ??)
abstract: The authors present some developments of unconventional AC drives. The project looked at in particular is a railway locomotive with eight wheel-subsystems (WS). Each system is a wheel driven by its own motor, a PWM convertor and a microprocessor for digital control. AC drives are used with a power of 40 kW and frequency of 16 kHz.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Dielectromagnetics in reluctance and hybrid electrical step motors
publicationTitle: 1989 Fourth International Conference on Electrical Machines and Drives Conf. Publ. No. ??)
abstract: The authors prove the usability of dielectromagnetic material for magnetic cores of step motors. Two types of step motors are chosen for this purpose: the reluctance step motor with elementary step -150 degrees and static pull-in torque and the hybrid step motor with elementary step -1.8 degrees and static pull-in torque. Dielectromagnetic material is used in the rotors of the motors.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Axial magnetic forces in induction machines at twice line frequency
publicationTitle: 1989 Fourth International Conference on Electrical Machines and Drives Conf. Publ. No. ??)
abstract: Axial magnetic forces on the rotor and stator of an induction machine are due to variations in the magnetic energy stored in the air gap along the machine axis. A virtual displacement of the rotor along the axial direction, in which the magnetic permeance of the air gap changes, leads to a change in the energy stored in the magnetic field and also a force in the axial direction between the rotor and the stator. In actual practice, induction machines with imperfectly balanced phase currents and containing a dissymmetry, or unsymmetrical configuration, in their magnetic circuit across the diameter of the machine, are not uncommon. In such a machine the rotating pole magnetic field can produce an axial magnetic force at twice line frequency in addition to the normal steady-state axial force. In certain applications, the vibrations produced by such a machine may be intolerable and modifications may be required. The author analyzes two examples of twice line frequency axial magnetic forces that may be encountered in induction machines.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Optimization of permanent magnet machines with respect to torque and audible noise
publicationTitle: 1989 Fourth International Conference on Electrical Machines and Drives Conf. Publ. No. ??)
abstract: The electromagnetically generated audible noise of rotating electrical machines has gained considerable attention. The authors use the finite element technique to optimise a buried magnet permanent magnet machine with respect to audible noise and torque. The buried magnets are tangentially magnetized and set into radial slots in a steel rotor. The combination of such a motor and an inverter has all the characteristics required for an efficient low-speed drive system.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Permanent magnet synchronous motors-steady state and transient performance prediction
publicationTitle: 1989 Fourth International Conference on Electrical Machines and Drives Conf. Publ. No. ??)
abstract: It is often important to predetermine the dynamic characteristics of a supply-motor-load system in order to reduce the rotor speed variations. The classical method numerically solves the motor dynamic equations, including the supply and the driver, and takes into account different transient states. It generally needs a long calculation time. When the motor speed variations are relatively low, a much faster analytical method, based on a double harmonic decomposition, is introduced instead of the numerical method. The analytical calculation method is first presented with its limits and basic hypothesis. Then, both numerical and analytical methods are used in different applications, as for instance pointing out the skewing effect on a given motor.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Motor and inverter design criteria for variable-speed and vector controlled AC drives
publicationTitle: 1989 Fourth International Conference on Electrical Machines and Drives Conf. Publ. No. ??)
abstract: The robustness, reliability and lack of maintenance requirements of cage induction motors make them an ideal choice for variable-speed drive applications. The authors identify some of the design parameters which affect the overall system behaviour. For the motor, consideration is given to: choice of base frequency, voltage/frequency profile, rotor slot shape, ventilation arrangements and lamination material. For the inverter: voltage ratings, choice of switching frequency for different control strategies and the selection of power devices will be discussed. The validity of the above design approach is demonstrated by results taken from actual designs, many of which are implemented in production equipment.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: The accurate modelling of large synchronous generators
publicationTitle: 1989 Fourth International Conference on Electrical Machines and Drives Conf. Publ. No. ??)
abstract: A digital model has been developed which accurately simulates the behaviour of synchronous generators, by taking saturation into account. The model is based on a simple equivalent circuit the parameters of which, including those describing saturation, are readily available from standard tests. The model's performance has been verified over a wide range of operating conditions using a microalternator. Beyond this, its validity has been checked in terms of practical generators, by successfully replicating the results of the Northfleet tests and works tests performed on a 660 MW machine. These tests and those on the micromachine revealed the need to include changes due to saturation, on a step by step basis in the modelling process in order to achieve accurate predictions of machine performance.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Calculation of temperature rises due to conductor losses in a radially-cooled turbogenerator rotor
publicationTitle: 1989 Fourth International Conference on Electrical Machines and Drives Conf. Publ. No. ??)
abstract: The rotor windings of large generators are usually cooled by hydrogen flowing through ducts within the winding. A detailed computer model, ROTH, has been developed to predict asymmetric temperature distributions. The original version was limited to rotors with axial cooling, but now it has been extended to handle radially-cooled rotors. The approximate method for estimating thermal bend has also been greatly improved. The author describes these enhancements, and validates them by comparing them with a simplified analytical solution, with an independently developed computer program and with limited experimental data.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Soft start equipment with common current source inverter for several high voltage motors
publicationTitle: 1989 Fourth International Conference on Electrical Machines and Drives Conf. Publ. No. ??)
abstract: Today, there is an evergrowing demand for frequency control and soft starting of three-phase induction motors with squirrel-cages. In addition to new installations, constant speed or hard starting (direct on line) drive systems, installed many years ago, can be adapted to the new operation requirements. In these cases, frequency control or soft start equipment is added to the motor. Mainly two different systems for soft starting can be applied: the three phase AC power controller; and the frequency converter. In the following, the design and application of control and power electronics for such special soft start equipment with frequency converter is described.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Classification of vibration signatures of turbogenerators
publicationTitle: 1989 Fourth International Conference on Electrical Machines and Drives Conf. Publ. No. ??)
abstract: The authors develop intelligent signature analysis software driven by the run-down and run-up signatures of various classes of rotating machine. The prototype class reported is a class of 660MW, 2-pole turbogenerator rotors passing through production company overspeed test pit-in various states of service history. Shaft absolute vibrations are recorded on several planes inboard and outboard of two bearings, and this study is focussed on four planes which would also be accessible on site for follow-up studies.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Further advances in the design of 3-phase squirrel cage induction motors using an expert system
publicationTitle: 1989 Fourth International Conference on Electrical Machines and Drives Conf. Publ. No. ??)
abstract: The authors describe a new approach to the design of squirrel cage induction motors using an expert system. A diagnostic process is proposed where the expert system is fed with a set of performance characteristics, and it diagnoses any faults within this.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Control at low speed of an induction motor
publicationTitle: 1989 Fourth International Conference on Electrical Machines and Drives Conf. Publ. No. ??)
abstract: The authors describe the design of a controller for a standard induction motor intended for application as a servo drive. The investigation was motivated by the fact that this type of motor is low in price as well as robust. The authors start with the fundamentals of an induction motor equipped with angular velocity control by means of a voltage source invertor. The fast control of torque and angular velocity necessitates the use of a dynamic flux controller. From the experiments performed it could be concluded that control of the motor by means of a standard voltage source invertor was not satisfactory since under quickly changing angular velocities the magnetic flux could not be kept at a constant level. It is shown that the control of torque and velocity in that case is too slow and also restricted, specially at the lower velocities, due to oscillations occurring in the flux.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Replacement of mechanical transmissions by synchronised variable electrical speed drives
publicationTitle: 1989 Fourth International Conference on Electrical Machines and Drives Conf. Publ. No. ??)
abstract: The replacement of mechanical transmission by synchronised variable speed drives is becoming an increasing trend for process control machinery. The introduction of this technology will require the application of new techniques which are currently being developed. The key to the new emerging design techniques is the selection of drives, and the prediction of, and improvement in, performance by use of simulation. It is shown how to compare drives and guide-lines have been presented to their selection. A case study has shown how it has been possible to more than double the performance of a system by use of simulation as a design tool.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: An alternator using a high temperature superconductor for field excitation
publicationTitle: 1989 Fourth International Conference on Electrical Machines and Drives Conf. Publ. No. ??)
abstract: The authors describe the construction and performance of an alternator using YBaCuO high temperature superconductor for field excitation. The excitation winding consist of 15 turns of superconducting wire encapsulated in wax. Tests are carried out at a generator speed of 1500 rev/min to give a 3-phase 50 Hz output.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Improved methods for inter-relating equivalent circuits and frequency-response data for synchronous machines
publicationTitle: 1989 Fourth International Conference on Electrical Machines and Drives Conf. Publ. No. ??)
abstract: The authors look at the mathematical modelling of the transient behaviour of turbogenerators from static small-signal measurements of frequency response characteristics. Fitting 2-axis equivalent circuits to measured data is discussed and attention is focussed on the d-axis. Arguments are advanced to show that established methods of fitting are open to criticism in a number of respects.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: The importance of complete drive train analysis for brushless salient pole motor drives
publicationTitle: 1989 Fourth International Conference on Electrical Machines and Drives Conf. Publ. No. ??)
abstract: It is important that a shaft train torsional analysis is carried out for all systems driven by synchronous motors. During starting, either by direct on-line or by using a variable frequency supply, the motor generates oscillatory air gap torques which excite a torsional response throughout the shaft system. The authors show that by implementing a torsional response study for a salient pole motor at an early stage in the design of a shaft system, high oscillatory torques can be avoided.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Design of the best windings of a machine to obtain a radial force
publicationTitle: 1989 Fourth International Conference on Electrical Machines and Drives Conf. Publ. No. ??)
abstract: The authors design the best windings for an electric machine, which can provide a radial force. They include a presentation of the mathematical method for computing the radial force: the formula of the magnetic pressure over the airgap is modified to use the Fourier distribution of the equivalent airgap currents. The final force is obtained by summing the harmonics. An irregular airgap can be taken into account. The radial force is then computed with various windings, or rotor eccentricity. The influence of the commutation from one coil to the next (discrete distribution of airgap currents) to obtain a revolving force, is also computed.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: An unmanned tracked hybrid vehicle
publicationTitle: 1989 Fourth International Conference on Electrical Machines and Drives Conf. Publ. No. ??)
abstract: The authors describe the application of a pair of brushless motors as the drive system for a small multi-purpose hybrid tracked vehicle developed for defence purposes. Experimentally obtained results are used to define certain of the vehicle characteristics, and to increase confidence in the accuracy of predictions obtained from a mathematical model of the system. The encouraging performance of a prototype vehicle has led to an investigation, based on the system model, of the advantages of a hybrid drive system for large reconnaissance and weapons platforms. This requires the model to be extended to include the forces involved during motion of the vehicle when cornering using skid steering.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Computer aided analysis of a DC brushless motor by means of a finite element technique
publicationTitle: 1989 Fourth International Conference on Electrical Machines and Drives Conf. Publ. No. ??)
abstract: The analysis of permanent magnet DC brushless motors can be conveniently performed by means of the finite element method, which gives the magnetic field distribution in complicate geometries taking into account the properties of saturable materials. Some facilities of the proposed computer aided analysis package are presented. The motor is analyzed both at rated and no-load operating conditions evaluating torque-angle curves, induction waveforms in the teeth region, and induced emf diagrams. The overload conditions are investigated to estimate the localized magnetic saturation and the demagnetizing effects on permanent magnets. The computed results are found to be in satisfactory agreement with the experimental ones.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Conception, optimization and realization of extra flat DC linear motors
publicationTitle: 1989 Fourth International Conference on Electrical Machines and Drives Conf. Publ. No. ??)
abstract: The authors present a method to determine the optimal electro-mechanical parameters of DC linear electrical motors containing permanent magnets. Static models for magnets and movable coils are investigated to determine optimal choice of structure, mechanical and electric parameters.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: A modified static Kraemer system operated as a variable speed induction generator
publicationTitle: 1989 Fourth International Conference on Electrical Machines and Drives Conf. Publ. No. ??)
abstract: A static Kraemer system with a converter extended by a controllable freewheeling circuit is described. Due to the freewheeling circuit, the converter can be operated with cos phi /sub 1/=1 or in an overexcited range. Two different control schemes for the freewheeling circuit are presented, a simple control scheme, permitting minimisation of fundamental reactive power and a control scheme, employing pulse pattern techniques to minimise fundamental reactive power and harmonic distortion. To produce near sinusoidal inverter output currents, a filter was designed to enhance the performance of the freewheeling circuit with the pulse pattern control scheme. Experimental results obtained from a small test drive (11 kW) are presented.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Transient behaviour of a three-phase slip-ring induction machine following a short supply interruption
publicationTitle: 1989 Fourth International Conference on Electrical Machines and Drives Conf. Publ. No. ??)
abstract: A coupled finite-element and circuits method has been described that can model the transient electrical and mechanical behaviour of slip-ring induction motors. The general technique is capable of modelling rotor and stator slotting effects and includes saturation of the magnetic circuit. A simple means of prediction the initial steady-state conditions of the motor has been outlined, resulting in a significant reduction in the overall solution time. The method has been used to demonstrate the transient behaviour of a slip-ring motor following disconnection from the supply. The effect of saturation on the steady-state full-load stator phase currents has also been demonstrated. The influence of the rotor currents following a disconnection up to two cycles of the supply has been shown to influence the initial negative torque normally present following a normal supply connection at speed.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>
